title: Hui-neng's Flag
koan_text: Two monks were arguing about the temple flag waving in the wind. One said, The flag moves. The other said, The wind moves. They argued back and forth but could not agree. Hui-neng, the sixth patriarch, said: Gentlemen! It is not the flag that moves. It is not the wind that moves. It is your mind that moves. The two monks were struck with awe.
commentary: It is not the wind, not the flag, not the mind. Where do you see the Patriarch's true meaning? If you see it intimately, you will see the two monks buying iron while trying to get gold.
commentary_2: Hui-neng spoke to cut off their dualistic arguing. If you say the mind moves, you fall into a trap. If you say it doesn't move, you miss the point completely.
verse:
Wind, flag, and mind moving together,
All talk falls short of the mark.
Only knowing how to open the mouth,
He completely missed the great path.

title: Kill the Buddha
koan_text: If you meet the Buddha on the road, kill him.
commentary: If you want to have the correct view of Zen, do not let yourselves be deceived by others. Whatever you encounter, either within or without, kill it immediately. If you meet a Buddha, kill the Buddha.
commentary_2: This is a warning against attachment to concepts, even holy ones. To cling to an external image of 'the Buddha' is an obstacle to realizing your own innate Buddha-nature.
verse:
To cut through the holy and the mundane alike,
The sharp blade leaves no trace behind.
When the external illusion is totally destroyed,
The real home appears right before your eyes.

title: Kegon's Broken Mirror
koan_text: A monk asked Kegon, How does an enlightened one return to the ordinary world? Kegon replied, A broken mirror never reflects again; fallen flowers never go back to the old branches.
commentary: Once a person has fully awakened, their old illusions are shattered completely. They cannot return to a state of ignorance, just as a shattered mirror can never project a perfect, undivided reflection.
commentary_2: Returning to the world does not mean repeating the old delusion. It means acting freely within the world without being bound by it ever again.
verse:
The shattered mirror yields no false image,
The fallen blossom leaves the ancient bough.
He returns to the marketplace with empty hands,
Yet everything he touches turns to pure gold.

title: Shuzan's Short Staff
koan_text: Shuzan held out his short staff and said, If you call this a short staff, you oppose its reality. If you do not call it a short staff, you ignore the fact. Now what do you wish to call this?
commentary: If you call it a short staff, you are caught in words. If you do not call it a short staff, you are turning away from the physical reality. It cannot be spoken, and it cannot be ignored.
commentary_2: Shuzan holds up the immediate world before your face. He traps you in a dilemma to force your mind past intellectual classifications.
verse:
Holding up the staff, he issues a command,
Life and death depend entirely on your word.
Opposition or ignorance both bring deep shame,
Even a quick response fails to escape.

title: The Many Reduced to One
koan_text: When the many are reduced to one, to what is the one reduced?
commentary: People understand the concept that all diverse things are part of a single reality. But they get stuck on that 'one.' You must go a step further and see where even unity disappears.
commentary_2: Chao-chou answered this elsewhere by saying, 'When I was in Ch'ing-chou, I made a cloth robe that weighed seven pounds.' He brought an abstract question right back to everyday material reality.
verse:
He asks about the one to find the source,
But the old master responds with a heavy robe.
If you try to weigh it on a logical scale,
You will remain trapped in words forever.

title: Haryo's Way
koan_text: A monk asked Master Haryo, What is the way? Haryo said, An open-eyed man falling into the well.
commentary: Haryo doesn't give a peaceful or comfortable definition of spiritual path. It is a total, clear-eyed immersion where you lose all control and drop straight down.
commentary_2: To walk the path is to plunge into reality without hesitation, fully aware of what you are doing, yet totally throwing yourself away.
verse:
An open-eyed man plunging into the deep well,
He doesn't cry out or look for a rope.
In the place where there is no bottom to hold him,
The clear spring water washes him clean.

title: Manjusri Outside the Gate
koan_text: One day as Manjusri stood outside the gate, the Buddha called to him, Manjusri, Manjusri, why do you not enter? Manjusri replied, I do not see myself as outside. Why enter?
commentary: If there is no division between inside and outside, entering is an illusion. Manjusri understands that the truth is completely borderless.
commentary_2: The Buddha asks a simple question to let Manjusri expose the absolute wholeness of reality, where no threshold actually exists.
verse:
Inside and outside are names for a dream,
What threshold is there for the wise to cross?
The ancient gate stands open day and night,
Yet not a single person has ever stepped through.

title: Two Monks, Two Blinds
koan_text: After taking the high seat to preach to the assembly, Fa-yen raised his hand and pointed to the bamboo blinds. Two monks went over and rolled them up in the same way. Fa-yen said, One gains, one loses.
commentary: Asks which monk really gained and which lost. If you can answer, you have the eye of the teacher. He adds a warning against trying to settle it by logic.
commentary_2: Both acted identically, yet the master divides them cleanly into gain and loss to see if you judge by appearances or touch the absolute essence.
verse: The blinds go up and the whole sky appears, but he says even the sky is not the point and you should not get stuck in it.

title: The Leaking Roof
koan_text: As the roof was leaking, a zen Master told two monks to bring something to catch the water. One brought a tub, the other a basket. The first was severely reprimanded, the second highly praised.
commentary: The tub tries to hold and collect the water, acting out of a mind that hoards. The basket lets the water flow through completely, capturing the true spirit of emptiness.
commentary_2: Zen rewards the action that matches absolute impermanence over the action that tries to store things up inside rigid boundaries.
verse:
One gathers the rain in a wooden frame,
One lets it stream through bamboo mesh.
To hold it tight is to lose the flow,
To let it go fills the entire universe.

title: Chao-chou in the Snow
koan_text: One day Chao-chou fell down in the snow, and called out, Help me up! Help me up! A monk came and lay down beside him. Chao-chou got up and went away.
commentary: The monk did not try to play the savior or lecture the master. By lying down right next to him, he entered the same exact reality, meeting him completely without pretense.
commentary_2: Chao-chou's test was met perfectly. When the monk joined him on the frozen ground, the lesson was over, and Chao-chou simply walked away.
verse:
Fallen in the snow, crying for a hand,
The companion arrives and shares the cold earth.
No words are spoken, no help is given,
Yet the two of them walk the very same road.

title: The Golden Wind
koan_text: A monk asks Ummon what happens when the leaves fall and the trees are bare. Ummon says: "Body exposed in the golden wind."
commentary: The monk's question is a trap. He is asking whether, once everything falls away, anything is left. Ummon refuses both "yes" and "no" and points at what is plainly there.
commentary_2: When all temporary structures and false identities decay, the absolute reality is completely exposed. There is nowhere left to hide, and nothing left to protect.
verse: Praises the answer's clean, wide-open quality. The imagery stays in autumn: wind, bare branches, and a figure with nothing left to hide behind.

title: Following the Spring
koan_text: Master Chosha returns from a walk. The head monk asks where he went. "Following the spring grasses, then back with the falling blossoms." The monk says, "That's very much like spring." Chosha replies, "Better than the autumn dew on the lotus."
commentary: Points out that Chosha's answer is poetry that also dodges the question. The head monk's "like spring" is a compliment that gets turned around.
commentary_2: Chosha takes the monk past simple seasonal descriptions. He points straight toward a timeless state that stays clear and bright long after the beautiful things fade away.
verse: Celebrates the season itself, with grasses, blossoms, and a feeling that spring is wandering in the master's own mind.

title: The Flower and the Dream
koan_text: A high official tells Nansen that a sage once said heaven, earth, and he were of one root, with all things one body. Nansen points to a peony in the garden and says: "People these days look at this flower as if in a dream."
commentary: The official quotes a lofty teaching about oneness, and Nansen deflates it by pointing at an ordinary flower. Engo's warning is that you can recite "all things are one" while sleepwalking past the peony in front of you.
commentary_2: Intellectual concepts of unity are still a separation from life. Nansen demands that the official wake up and see the actual, physical flower blooming right before his eyes.
verse: Describes the scene in a gentle, hazy way, and it ends up leaving the listener to ask who exactly is dreaming.

title: The Girl Whose Soul Departed
koan_text: Seijo's soul separated from her body. Her father had promised her to one man, but she loved another. She fled with her lover and lived with him for five years. Years later, she went home with her children, and the father said she had been lying ill in bed all that time. Which one was the real Seijo?
commentary: If you truly see the one real person, you will know that moving from one body to another is like passing through a roadside inn. If you can't, he tells you not to rush and not to be caught off guard when the elements break apart.
commentary_2: This case shatters our ordinary ideas about a solid, singular identity. It forces you to look for the true nature that isn't divided by space, body, or time.
